title: Apply Function VS Vectorized Operations
text:
In Class I have been learning about how to utilize Pandas in my data cleaning and analysis. One of the earliest functions we learned is the .apply() function. This is a super useful function that we can use to make changes to all of our rows in one call.
The downside is, it isn’t always the most efficient. This often wont make a huge difference but if we are working with large data sets, it can cut your run time down by a lot.
In this article, I hope to explain:

How does .apply() work?
When should we use it?
What is the alternative?

Having an understanding of apply() and its shortcomings will help you spend less time waiting on your computer and make you a better Data Scientist




The .apply() function takes another function and applies it to each row or column in a Series or DataFrame.
If it sounds like a loop, that’s because it kind of is one.

.apply() executes Python code row-by-row.

This is the main shortcoming, rather than doing things all at once, its going through, one at a time and this takes time while simultaneously not allowing your computer to work as hard as it could using other methods.This is why the difference is much more noticeable on larger datasets.


import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "score": [72, 88, 95, 60, 83]
})

def pass_fail(x):
    return "Pass" if x >= 70 else "Fail"

df["result"] = df["score"].apply(pass_fail)
df
This is a great use for apply(), it keeps the code intuitive and since it isn’t very large, we dont even notice the extra time it takes.





.apply() makes the most sense when:

When your logic is complex and hard to vectorize
You have conditional transformations
You are in the EDA phase of your analysis
Your dataset is small enough that you aren’t worried about how long it takes



def categorize(score):
    if score >= 90:
        return "A"
    elif score >= 80:
        return "B"
    elif score >= 70:
        return "C"
    else:
        return "Below C"

df["grade"] = df["score"].apply(categorize)
df
Similarly to the previous example, this helps the code to be easy to read and understand.





The biggest issue is size.
.apply() as mentioned before works almost like a loop, meaning it performs the operations over and over where as other methods can do it all at once. It still does it very quickly so unless you’re dealing with hundreds of rows it probably wont be a problem but sometimes we are working with millions of rows and that can have a huge difference.
An example of .apply() not being ideal is finding a mean:
\[
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i
\]
Being able to write it as a simple formula is a big hint that alternative options will be feasible and doing something like this in a loop will take forever. So what are your options?




Bringing us back to Linear algebra and using vectors can help us do some of our computations way more efficiently.
You may be thinking that this is great for numbers but we can also use it with boolean data.


df["result_vectorized"] = df["score"] >= 70
df
This adds a new column to our dataframe which we can compare to our earlier results, this time it returns True or False which is a little bit less readable but often we would want it that way anyway. Another limitation is that our grade column is going to be much harder to replicate. As you can see by the code though, once you’re familiar with how it works, its more concise and easier to read.
The reason this is so much faster is because it converts the columns into vectors and does everything all at once rather than every row individually.
Since optimization can be really important, Pandas has published official documentation to improve performance. Link Here.





{fig-alt=“Image comparing loops (Apply function) vs vectorized logic}
Figure: Vectorized operations operate on entire arrays at once, rather than looping through rows individually.




Before using the .apply() function:

Is this logic simple?
Is there a built-in Pandas function for this?
Would a Boolean response work?

If you answer yes to any of these, consider avoiding .apply()




.apply() is great and extremely useful in many ways but it isn’t the best tool for every job.
Steps to take:

Utilize built-in Pandas methods whenever possible

Try Vectorized operations
Use .apply() for complex custom transformations

Even if you’re currently working with smaller data where efficiency isn’t a huge priority, consider practicing more efficient methods to build those skills and to be ready for larger datasets.

title: A Permission-Aware Market & News Data Portal
text: I designed and built a PostgreSQL-backed data portal that serves stock-market and financial-news data to three tiers of users — anonymous guests, signed-in members, and admins — with what each user sees enforced inside the database itself. The database runs on Supabase, and the interface is a static site with live charts, an interactive article map, a personal watchlist, and a read-only SQL console.
crumbs: A Permission-Aware Market & News Data Portal

title: A Permission-Aware Market & News Data Portal
text:
The Problem
This project grew out of a personal process I actually run: investment research. I collect market data (prices, filings, earnings, analyst ratings, insider transactions) and a corpus of scraped financial-news articles that I enrich with ticker mentions, sentiment scores, and embeddings. Until now the data only lived in a warehouse I could reach from my own machines — useful to me, invisible to everyone else, and impossible to share safely.
That sharing problem turned out to be the interesting one:

Mixed licensing. Some sources are public (SEC filings, Wikipedia’s S&P 500 list, exchange symbol directories, my own derived data), but the market data vendors I use license their data for personal use only. I can show trends computed from that data — I cannot hand out the raw numbers.
Mixed audiences. A recruiter or classmate browsing my site is a guest; a signed-in member should see more; I (the admin) need everything. One static page can’t serve all three without somewhere to enforce the rules.
No editing surface. Members had no way to interact with the data — no way to keep a list of tickers they care about or shape their own view.

The domain therefore has two parts: securities and everything recorded about them, and articles and everything derived from them. Access control is a real requirement of the app, but accounts and permissions are application plumbing — they live outside the domain model.

Users

Guest — no account; explores public data (index composition, filings activity, headlines, sentiment aggregates, the article map).
Member — signed in; additionally sees derived trends computed from licensed data (rebased sector price indexes, earnings beat rates, analyst mix, insider direction, sentiment-vs-move statistics) and keeps a personal watchlist.
Admin — me; additionally reads raw rows (full OHLCV series, article detail with model rationales) and runs read-only SQL against the warehouse.
crumbs: A Permission-Aware Market & News Data Portal

title: A Permission-Aware Market & News Data Portal
text:
Analysis and Design

Domain description
A Security is issued by a Company and listed on an Exchange. Each security accumulates daily prices, earnings events, corporate actions, analyst estimates/consensus/price targets, institutional ownership, and insider activity. Membership in a stock index changes over time, so IndexMembership records when a security was added and removed and which sector it belongs to.
An Outlet publishes Articles. An article can mention many securities and a security can appear in many articles, so TickerMention is an association class carrying how often the ticker appeared, whether it was in the headline, and how it was found. Each mention is scored by models (SentimentScore), and each article can hold Embeddings reduced to EmbeddingProjections for the article map.
User accounts, roles, and sessions are provided by the application’s auth layer (Supabase Auth) and are deliberately outside the domain model.


Domain Class Diagram



UML domain class diagram — 22 classes including the TickerMention association class


22 classes including the TickerMention association class, with multiplicities on every association. The diagram was generated by a small Python script that lays out boxes and orthogonal connectors explicitly to minimize crossing lines.


Key design decisions

The database enforces permissions, not the page. The site is static — its HTML is public and contains no data. Every read goes through a SECURITY DEFINER function in a dedicated portal schema that resolves the caller’s tier (Supabase Auth JWT → app.users.role, defaulting to guest) and returns only what that tier may see. The anonymous API role has no grants on the data schemas at all.
“Derived” is a first-class access level. Between “invisible” and “readable” sits derived: the member tier sees structure and server-transformed trends (indexed prices, percentages, medians, counts) but never raw vendor values. This is how licensed market data can legitimately power a public demo. Member trend functions aggregate inside Postgres before any JSON leaves the server.
Article bodies stay out of the database. Only headline, URL, and derived rows are stored — cheaper, and it respects publisher copyright.
Sentiment attaches to the mention, not the article. An article can say good things about one ticker and bad things about another; scoring the article–ticker pair is what makes per-ticker sentiment meaningful.



Deliberately out of scope

Trading — no order placement or brokerage connection; this is a research tool.
Real-time data — end-of-day prices only; no tick stream.
Anything but US equities — no options, futures, forex, or non-US listings; daily prices cover the S&P 500 universe, 2015–2025.
Full article text — copyright and storage; headline + link + derived rows only.
Your own portfolio — positions, cost basis, and transactions are not modeled.
Accounts and permissions — user accounts, roles, and sessions are the app’s auth layer, separate from the domain tables.
User-generated content — no posting, comments, or social features.
crumbs: A Permission-Aware Market & News Data Portal

title: A Permission-Aware Market & News Data Portal
text:
The Solution

The database
The design is implemented on Supabase in three data schemas plus a published API surface:







Schema
Contents




stocks
exchanges, companies, securities, index_memberships, daily_prices, sec_filings, earnings_events, corporate_actions, analyst_consensus/estimates/price_targets, insider_roster/transactions, institutional_ownership


news
outlets, articles (metadata only), article_tickers, sentiment_scores, article_embeddings, embedding_projections


app
roles, users, role_permissions, sessions, watchlist_entries — application plumbing (auth + member watchlists), outside the domain model


portal
~20 SECURITY DEFINER functions — the only surface the browser can call — plus a private portal_cache materialized view for precomputed trends



Foreign keys tie the graph together exactly as the diagram shows: every fact table references securities.ticker; article_tickers joins articles.id to securities.ticker (the TickerMention association class); sentiment_scores references a mention. The member watchlist (app.watchlist_entries) joins each signed-in user to the securities they follow — an application record kept deliberately thin, since the domain itself doesn’t model accounts.
The permission layer is table-driven: app.role_permissions maps each role to resource patterns (schema.*, schema.table, schema.table.column) with levels none < derived < read < write, most specific rule wins. Guest sees the public columns, member adds derived trends, admin sees raw values.
For grading, a standalone, re-runnable build script (is302_schema.sql) creates an equivalent is302 schema implementing the domain model (the stocks + news tables), indexes on the commonly filtered columns (ticker, dates, article/source links), a reporting view that joins articles → mentions → sentiment → securities → outlets into one per-ticker news summary, and sample data for every table.


The application
The portal is a static Quarto site on GitHub Pages. Every chart calls a portal.* RPC; sections that need a higher tier are simply not rendered for lower tiers.

Sign-in page

The Stocks dashboard as a guest — S&P 500 sector composition with the tier badge visible (“GUEST / Browsing as guest”). Members get additional derived-trend panels below this fold, plus the watchlist form; admins get the raw OHLCV panel:

title: A Permission-Aware Market & News Data Portal
text:
Insights
The analysis notebook asks the obvious question of this data: does a news mention’s sentiment predict what the stock does next? It joins every scored ticker mention to the ticker’s next 21 daily closes, computes 1-, 5-, and 20-trading-day forward returns, and regresses return on sentiment score.



Left: mean forward returns after a mention, by sentiment label. Right: each mention’s sentiment score vs. its realized 5-day move, with a fitted regression line.


The honest answer: no. Across 854 scored mentions with enough price history, the OLS slope of the 5-day forward return on sentiment score is +0.05% per unit of score — statistically indistinguishable from zero (p = 0.897, R² = 0.000). The logistic model agrees (p = 0.584): it puts the chance of an up week at about 54% after a maximally negative mention and about 50% after a maximally positive one — backwards, if anything.
Two quieter findings are more interesting than the headline:

Everything drifts up together. Mean 5-day returns are positive for every label (+0.5% negative, +1.3% neutral, +0.6% positive) because the coverage universe is S&P 500 names in a mostly-rising market. Neutral mentions averaged the best returns — routine coverage of names already trending, not sentiment causing the move.
The score measures tone, not edge. The null result is a useful validation: the sentiment pipeline is describing how articles read, and nothing more — which is exactly what a compliance-sensitive aggregate should be.

Caveats: mentions cluster (the same event is covered by many outlets, so rows aren’t independent), the sample tilts toward large caps with the most coverage, and association is not a tradable signal.
crumbs: A Permission-Aware Market & News Data Portal

title: A Permission-Aware Market & News Data Portal
text:
Reflection
The hard part was not drawing the diagram — it was the permission model. A static site means anyone can open DevTools and read whatever the API returns, so “hiding values in a chart” is not security. The honest design was to make the database the enforcer: one API schema of SECURITY DEFINER functions, a table of permission rules, and — the subtle piece — a “derived” tier that returns transformations (rebased indexes, percentages, counts) computed server-side rather than the raw licensed values. Getting that clean took a redesign: the first version gave members raw read access to vendor tables.
What I learned: treating “who may see what” as data (rows in role_permissions, resolved per-call) instead of code made the tiers cheap to change and audit, and it produced the permission-aware data dictionary for free. I also learned how much domain modeling pays off — the TickerMention association class is the single decision that makes per-ticker sentiment coherent.
Next: more outlets and a larger corpus, alerting on watchlist tickers, and exploring whether the derived-tier trick generalizes to other licensed datasets. If I did it again I’d design the permission rules earlier — retrofitting them onto existing tables was the most error-prone step.

title: Matthew Conger
text:
About me
I’m a Statistics major (Data Science emphasis) at BYU, graduating April 2027.
This past summer I interned at ProdataKey as a data analyst. My main project was a dbt + Snowflake pipeline that classifies dealer accounts by growth trend, with Tableau dashboards on top for the sales team. Before that I spent a year as a research assistant in the Marriott School of Business — mostly logistic regression on survey data about how employees perceive AI. Before that, a year on a seven-person front-end team at the business school writing React and TypeScript.
The common thread is that I like the whole process: getting data that wasn’t meant to be analyzed, cleaning it properly, and ending with an answer someone can use. title: Data Acquisition For Reporting Analysis
text:
This data comes from two main sources. I used Yahoo Finance’s API system to get historic data for all companies currently traded on the NASDAQ stock exchange. The other key element of this dataset is the dates that these companies filed their annual and quarterly reports, to get this I used the SEC EDGAR API system as well as a smaller API to convert ticker symbol (unique stock identifiers) into CIKs (a numeric unique identifier) so that I could request data from the SEC system.
I then combined and summarized these two sources into one large dataset which I will use to answer my question.

The other key element of this dataset is the dates that these companies filed their annual and quarterly reports, to get this I used the SEC EDGAR API system as well as a smaller API to convert ticker symbol (unique stock identifiers) into CIKs (a numeric unique identifier) so that I could request data from the SEC system.
I then combined and summarized these two sources into one large dataset which I will use to answer my question.

title: Data Acquisition For Reporting Analysis
text:
Motivating Question

Do stock prices fully adjust on the day of an earnings announcement, or is there post-earnings drift?

When companies announce their earnings, this has a direct effect on the stock price. For a long time it was accepted that this had an effect over the course of a few weeks after the report was published, this is what the post-earnings drift refers to. In more recent times due to the speed that the internet allows these reports to circulate, there are opinions that this adjustment is now absorbed into the stock price much more quickly (in this case synonymous with efficiently) some even believe that the price adjustment happens within the first day.
My aim is to compare the time of adjustment between pre 2010 markets and 2010-2025 markets to find if there is a statistically significant difference between the two.

title: Data Acquisition For Reporting Analysis
text:
Data Sources
This project uses two primary data sources:

SEC EDGAR API – used to obtain filing dates

Yahoo Finance API – used to obtain historical stock price data

Both data sources are widely used in financial research and are publicly accessible.
I also made sure to follow the guidelines given in the API documentation for each to make sure everything was as it should be. Also the fact that they have APIs in place is evidence that they want this data to be accessible.

SEC EDGAR API
The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission has an API available to access the data from their EDGAR system I used it to get:

filing types (10-K, 10-Q, etc.)
filing dates

SEC EDGAR API Documentation


Yahoo Finance
Yahoo Finance is where I got my historic data. It is a bit different since instead of using the normal requests package, Yahoo Finance has their own Python package to request data.
yfinance GitHub Repository



Storing the data
For the historic stock market data, I saved each company’s data as its own CSV where the name was ticker.csv so I could look through the directory and get any companies information.
For the filing dates, I saved the data in a JSON file with each company ticker as an object with two objects inside it with the two types of documents filed and a list of the dates those were filed.



Combine the Datasets
To combine the data I loaded the JSON file with the filing dates then looped through each ticker, and for each one, I retrieved the associated csv file containing the data for that company. Then for each company I went through each filing date.
For each filing date I found 5 values: -The percent change in stock price on that day -The percent change in stock price on the next day -The average percent change in stock price from 2 to 4 days after -The average percent change in stock price from 5 to 10 days after -The average percent change in stock price from 11 to 30 days after
Each one is a column along with the company ticker and the filing date.

title: Post-Earnings Announcement Drift in S&P 500 Companies, 2015–2025
text:
Do stock prices fully adjust on the day of an earnings announcement, or does a measurable post-announcement window remain? This report examines the behavior of stock-return variance in the days surrounding SEC quarterly and annual filings for S&P 500 companies from 2015 to 2025, applying the cumulative sum of squares methodology of Inclan & Tiao (1994) within a functional data framework.
Written as the final project for BYU’s advanced technical-writing course — a professionally formatted analytical report with a letter of transmittal, executive summary, figures, and an MLA 9 bibliography.



Read it: Full report (PDF)
Analysis code is private — available on request. pead_analysis.R reproduces every figure.
Statistics Finance R Technical Writing




The supporting pipeline: filing dates and prices come from the Post-Earnings Drift data acquisition project; the functional-data analysis is written up separately in FDA — Filings & Intraday Returns.
